name: Douglas Gray
title: Principal Applied Scientist
about: Research scientist who has led teams and shipped at global scale: the vision-language systems behind Amazon Lens and visual navigation features in Amazon product search reach hundreds of millions of customers. I believe world-model-grounded, full-duplex interfaces are where computing is heading, and want to work on the hardest problems to get there: multimodal reasoning, agentic retrieval, generative models, and real-time interfaces.
_about_extended: Research scientist who has led teams and shipped vision-language systems at global scale. My work at Amazon has been a series of incremental steps toward a longer-term conviction: that the next great leap in computing isn't a better chat interface, but full-duplex interaction — video, audio, and language flowing through systems that persistently model the world. I think world models are the key technology, and the problems I most want to work on are multimodal reasoning, agentic retrieval, generative models, and real-time interfaces. At Amazon I've led the vision-language systems behind Amazon Lens, which lets customers point a camera at anything and find it, along with visual navigation features in Amazon product search used by hundreds of millions of customers globally. My research has appeared at CVPR, KDD, ECCV, and WACV, and I've co-organized the Multimodal Representation and Retrieval workshop at SIGIR and ICCV.
location: Portola Valley, CA (near Palo Alto, 30 min south of SF)

bullets: Led Lens Live as principal technical lead — real-time visual search integrated with Rufus for product insights, deployed to tens of millions of customers.

Architected the mobile ML pipeline (on-device detection, tracking, and state management) enabling continuous low-latency product identification as customers scan; coordinated development across multiple VP orgs in four locations.
experience._notes: Transitioned to full IC focus in early 2025 to lead Lens Live end-to-end. Day-to-day technical lead coordinating across multiple VP orgs — Lens (Palo Alto), Rufus engineering and science (Palo Alto, Seattle, NYC), and Rufus product (London) — teams that often didn’t agree. Core technical contribution was the mobile client architecture: on-device object detection, object tracking, and session state management (a lightweight world model of the scene). Scene understanding work focused on product-market fit: short “pills” for customers to tap and ask questions, and taglines surfacing what’s distinctive about a product. Latency was a core challenge — the pipeline had to deliver results continuously in real time as the camera moved.

bullets: Led a team of up to 20 applied scientists and engineers; completed the transformation of Amazon Lens into a deep learning, embedding-based system matching against over 1 billion products, driving significant gains in CTR and usage.
Launched Visual Search Suggestions, multimodal search (image + text reformulation), and More Like This — growing the latter from zero to over 90% of Amazon search result pages.

Built and developed a high-performing research team across all levels; organized Amazon’s Computer Vision Conference (ACVC, 200+ attendees) and co-organized the Multimodal Representation and Retrieval workshop (MRR) at SIGIR and ICCV as lead organizer and advisor.
experience._notes: Core technical achievement was completing the Lens transformation: the deep learning embedding-based system grew to match against over 1 billion products across the full Amazon catalog, ultimately retiring the classical CV pipeline. Features launched: multimodal search (image + text reformulation), Visual Search Suggestions (image-based pivots in text autocomplete), and More Like This (visual similarity within search results, scaled from zero to 90%+ of search result pages). Built and promoted team members across all levels. Organized ACVC with 200+ attendees as lead organizer and as advisor in other years; co-organized the MRR workshop at SIGIR 2024 and ICCV 2025.

bullets: Led a team of up to 12 applied scientists and engineers; introduced deep learning to Amazon’s visual search stack from scratch — from first launch at ~100 categories, expanding to 100,000+ fine-grained search strings via query-log-trained models, then to instance-level matching against ~10M products — culminating in StyleSnap (2019) and StyleSnap for Home (2020).
experience._notes: The existing classical CV system matched against ~100M products but was architecturally limited to flat and printed objects and had reached its ceiling. This role built a deep learning visual search system from the ground up: first launch covered ~100 product categories; a query-log-trained model then expanded the output vocabulary to over 100,000 fine-grained search strings, mapping images to the most relevant terms from Amazon’s actual query traffic; then instance-level product matching within specific categories — apparel first, then home — against roughly 10 million specific products. The public milestones were StyleSnap (2019) and StyleSnap for Home (2020). The subsequent role completed the journey, scaling to over 1 billion products and retiring the classic CV pipeline entirely.

bullets: Early applied scientist on A9’s visual search team; built A9 Flow (AR-based multi-object product recognition and tracking, initially a standalone demo app), with the underlying recognition, tracking, and scene text/OCR libraries later integrated into both the Amazon mobile app and the Amazon Fire Phone. Also developed video content alignment tools that automated annotation workflows for the IMDB X-Ray feature. Classical CV in high-performance C++.
experience._notes: A9 Flow was an augmented reality shopping interface and technology demonstrator — recognized and tracked multiple products in the scene simultaneously, overlaying results in real time. The Flow libraries (recognition, tracking, scene text detection, OCR) were later integrated into the main Amazon app and the Amazon Fire Phone. OCR covered phone numbers, addresses, and business card scanning. Video work was with IMDB and what became the Prime Video team: built tools to automatically align visual content from video against existing annotations, saving the team from manually redoing timestamp work each time studios redelivered content (see video content alignment patent).

bullets: Research scientist at an early-stage computer vision startup; built a video content search engine and developed multimedia summarization products — automated news article summarization and story clustering, and a video summarization API — using SVD of hand-crafted features.
experience._notes: Recruited by a former NEC Labs manager after an internship there. Initial project was a video content search engine. After lead investor Max Palevsky died and most of the science team was laid off, the company pivoted to commercializing multimedia summarization technology licensed from NEC. Products included itwips.com (automated 5-line summaries of top news articles, with story/theme clustering) and iBlips (a video summarization API). Added novel IP including the news clustering approach and contributed UX design. All summarization was SVD-based on hand-crafted features. The company folded when the products didn’t gain commercial traction.

Did not finish: advisor’s departure, transitions through Smith Kettlewell Eye Research Institute and Akiira, and getting married made returning to grad school impractical. The two highly cited papers from this period: “Viewpoint Invariant Pedestrian Recognition with an Ensemble of Localized Features” (ECCV 2008, 1,953 citations) and “Evaluating Appearance Models for Recognition, Reacquisition, and Tracking” (PETS 2007, 1,380 citations). Combined: 3,333 citations as of early 2026.
